extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and municipal administration
extracted.subtask_description: A historical and practical survey of municipal functions in U.S. cities (street cleaning, lighting, transportation, waterworks, education, parks, recreation, public health) with examples and institutional guidance. Useful as an instructional summary for students and practitioners evaluating municipal policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for preparation of household wastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonel Waring made a contribution to the solution of the problem by laying down rules to be observed by private citizens in the preparation of their wastes for disposal, which require them to separate decaying vegetable matter from ashes and waste papers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens should separate decaying vegetable matter from ashes and waste papers; municipalities should establish plants for reduction of materials collected by street cleaners. Example: Cleveland (1907) collected and reduced 37,606 tons of garbage; cost $193,365.76; income from sale of products (mostly grease) $136,985.60, leaving $56,380.16 charged to taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal waste-treatment plants and revenue model
rubrics_metrics.description: All of our large cities now have plants for the treatment of wastes, and many of them derive considerable revenue by employing scientific methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess municipal waste treatment not only on sanitation outcomes but on potential product recovery and revenue; use cost/income accounting (example Cleveland 1907 figures) to evaluate burden on taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Street lighting as public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Street-lighting is more than a matter of public convenience or aesthetic appearance — it is a matter of public safety, being closely related to the prevention of crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating municipal lighting policy, prioritize safety and crime prevention effects in addition to convenience and aesthetic considerations; consider technological choices (gas vs electricity) in light of practicability and public safety benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and ownership choices for street lighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Public lighting developed from gas to electricity; municipalities relied on private corporations for gas but municipal ownership of electric-lighting plants is far more common and more successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare private franchise vs municipal ownership by historical performance (service, popularity, financial results). Note that municipal ownership experiments with gas were often unsuccessful/unpopular, whereas electric plant municipal ownership showed greater success (statistics of cities owning plants in 1903).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of private franchises for municipal utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of our municipalities have relied upon private corporations to supply gas for street illumination... Experiments in municipal ownership of gas-lighting plants in America do not appear to have been either successful or popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When granting franchises, consider long-term effects on municipal control and public welfare; examine alternatives such as municipal ownership, leasing, or regulated private operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal responsibility for mass transportation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities must deal with the gigantic problem of transporting thousands of passengers; practically all systems are in the control of private companies operating under franchises granted by the cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate transport systems for capacity, mode (surface, elevated, subway), and adapt municipal policy as population density increases; recognize historical transitions (horse-car → cable → electric → elevated/subway).

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental supervision and regulatory controls over street railways
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a marked tendency to exercise governmental supervision over municipal systems of transportation — to limit the franchises of street railway companies to a shorter term of years, to control the amount of capital stock issued, to require the issue of transfers, and, in some cities, to force the establishment of low fares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory levers include franchise term limits, capitalization controls, transfer policies, and fare regulation. Use these tools to protect public interest, ensure service continuity, and restrain monopoly abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks from corruption and overcapitalization in transport companies
rubrics_metrics.description: The development has been accompanied by corruption, extravagant methods, and overcapitalization, which make it difficult to establish any just and equitable system of supervision and control on a purely business basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for political and financial malpractices when designing oversight; anti-corruption safeguards and transparent financial review are necessary parts of municipal supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy and purity of municipal water supply
rubrics_metrics.description: The furnishing of an adequate supply of pure water takes high rank. Its relation to the health and comfort of the people in cities was early understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Water policy should prioritize public health (purity) and adequate quantity; investments are often large (more than two-thirds of municipal industry capital invested in waterworks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Per capita water consumption and management policy
rubrics_metrics.description: With the increased facilities for supply... there has been a steady rise in the daily per capita consumption... The larger consumption... is partially due to the liberal policy of waterworks management and partially to greater ingenuity in sanitary appliances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance liberal supply policies against waste/leakage; consider meters for private consumers to reduce neglect and leakage, but weigh social costs of discouraging free use versus benefits of conservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized water plants for specific municipal functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The question has recently been raised as to the advisability of constructing special plants for fighting fires and flushing down the streets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider separate infrastructure for high-demand uses (fire-fighting, street flushing) if general system cannot supply intermittently large volumes without compromising other needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal ownership of waterworks and risks of private franchises
rubrics_metrics.description: In the construction and operation of water plants we find a more extensive and more successful application of the principle of public ownership than in the case of any other municipal utility... The principle has made great headway because the cities have learned... that when a franchise is once granted to a private company it is difficult for the municipality to regain control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor municipal ownership for essential utilities due to long-term control and public benefit. Beware of private franchise terms that hamper later municipal reacquisition (example: Los Angeles 1868 thirty-year contract leading to costly legal battles and purchase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal expansion into social welfare activities
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been a growing demand for the city to undertake a large variety of activities which were once regarded as wholly outside the field of public enterprise... in the extension and development of popular education, in the planning of streets... in the provision of parks, playgrounds, and recreational centres, in the construction of public hospitals and sanitariums, the stricter supervision of the milk and food supply, and in a thousand other ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess municipal roles beyond traditional public works when industrial urban conditions create collective needs—use public resources to improve welfare, public health, and social infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of settlements and private investigations in municipal reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Through university settlements, students of social problems have come into actual contact with the sad realities... Private investigations into the wages and conditions of life... have made public concrete facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical social investigations and settlement work to inform municipal policy and reveal neglected problems that require public intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational system metrics and improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1870 to 1899 the enrolment of children in the elementary schools... increased from 7,500,000 to 15,000,000... The development of high schools belongs to a later period... the design, construction, artistic effect, and conveniences of our modern city schools... standards of scholarship required of teachers have also appreciated immeasurably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by enrolment, percent of school-age population enrolled, teacher workforce numbers, quality of facilities, and teacher training/standards. Track expansion of high schools and improvement in school buildings over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as social centres and expanded school functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The schools of our cities are slowly becoming social centres; the playground and recreational features are being developed; vacation schools... vocational schools... medical inspection... dental and medical clinics... open-air schools... lunch rooms where undernourished children may obtain food at a nominal cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design schools to serve broader social/health/vocational roles: include playgrounds, clinics, vocational training, and support services for undernourished or sick children to raise intellectual, physical and moral standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and powers of boards of education
rubrics_metrics.description: A board of education is created by law whose members are selected by the people, serve without pay, and have full legal power to establish and control free public schools... Each year they make estimates in detail of the amounts of money required... The money once appropriated is controlled by the board of education, who buy sites, build and repair schoolhouses, purchase supplies, and pay the necessary officers and teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate school governance by legal authority, selection method (elected/appointed), budgeting role, control over appropriated funds, and responsibility for management and hiring of executive officers (secretary, superintendent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adult education and night lecture programs
rubrics_metrics.description: New York City... has established a system of free night lectures in the public school buildings... called 'the people's university'... courses cover every important subject... A special effort is made to reach the foreign population... given in their native tongues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support lifelong learning via free night lectures; tailor offerings to immigrant populations by providing courses in native languages; coordinate with boards of education and supervisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public libraries and branch systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Our great cities... have been steadily developing the system of branch libraries which makes the books available to the inhabitants of every district... a large gift by Andrew Carnegie has made it possible... to erect and maintain... sixty-five branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote wide access through branch libraries; measure impact by circulation and branch coverage; leverage philanthropy while ensuring public funding and strategic placement to serve children and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and distribution of parks and playgrounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities are coming slowly to realize that the provision for healthful recreation... is a collective function... many small parks, conveniently scattered through the congested areas, are of far greater utility than wide areas on the outskirts... it is estimated that there is only one square foot of playground for each child in the metropoles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize many accessible small parks/playgrounds within congested neighborhoods rather than only large peripheral parks; plan for equitable geographic distribution to serve the poor and children who cannot pay transit fares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active programming and facilities in parks
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities are endeavoring to make the parks especially attractive by providing athletic sports, such as baseball, tennis, golf, and dancing. Many give band concerts in the parks... Cleveland gave thirty-seven Sunday and twenty-six evening band concerts... twenty baseball diamonds... eight public playgrounds equipped with swings, sand piles... under charge of athletic directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equip parks with diverse athletic, cultural, and supervised recreation programs; distribute events and facilities to give equal benefit to all parts of the city; employ athletic directors and staff to manage activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schoolyard playgrounds and seasonal recreational uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Boston has equipped the school yards as playgrounds for children... New York has a law requiring the provision of a playground with every new school building... In the winter time, Chicago, New York, Boston... flood the playgrounds and turn them into skating rinks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate playgrounds with schools and design for year-round uses (e.g., skating in winter); adopt legal requirements for playground provision in new school construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive recreational centers model (South Park Board example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The board established fourteen parks... provided ball fields, tennis courts, swimming pools, sand piles, swings, lagoons for rowing and skating, stands for band concerts, and outdoor gymnasiums... established indoor recreation buildings equipped with shower and plunge baths and lockers, and lunch, reading, club, and assembly rooms... in the winter time lectures, dancing, and musical entertainments are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing recreational policy, combine outdoor and indoor facilities, provide hygiene (showers, baths, lockers), multi-use assembly spaces, staffed athletic directors, and year-round programming to attract and retain diverse populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recreational instructors' objectives and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Extracts instruct instructors: 'the gymnasium and the athletic field are schools of character... the instructor should praise every tendency of a boy or girl to sacrifice himself or herself for the good of the team... Keep in mind that we are public servants...' and objectives: (1) take children from streets, (2) encourage wholesome use of idle hours, (3) encourage personal hygiene, (4) furnish wholesome amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recreational staff should aim to attract and hold participants, inculcate cooperation and civic virtues, promote hygiene (exercise and bathing), and plan programs to establish habitual use of facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal provision of public baths
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of the state of New York makes the construction of free baths obligatory upon cities with over 50,000 inhabitants and permissible for others... in 1908 the investment of New York in municipal baths amounted to $3,000,000, and eight large bathing places were in operation in Manhattan alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider public baths as part of public health infrastructure; use state obligations and investments as benchmarks; include swimming instruction and year-round accessibility where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of municipal reforms and linkage to broader economic issues
rubrics_metrics.description: These various experiments in municipal reform, valuable as they undoubtedly are, by no means solve the most fundamental problems of modern urban life; these problems are connected with the larger questions of poverty, industry, transportation, agriculture, and the development of our natural resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize municipal measures as necessary but not sufficient; coordinate municipal policy with state/national economic policy to address root causes like poverty and industrial structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcrowding as a measurable public-health problem
rubrics_metrics.description: At the outset there is the grave problem of overcrowding... in New York City the death rate, 16.5 per thousand in 1908, was higher than in Berlin or London... 'annual economic waste from preventable diseases in New York City ranges from $37,000,000 to $40,000,000' largely due to overcrowding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mortality and morbidity rates, and economic cost estimates of preventable disease, as key metrics for assessing the severity of overcrowding. Link policy responses (housing, wages, sanitation) to measurable health outcomes.
